messages.text: I’ll read the lane brief, make the coverage changes it calls for, and run the focused checks before handing back.

Both recursive walks have input-controlled depth. The comment classifier also accepts either quote style as a closing delimiter. I’ll make the walks iterative and add regressions through RQL searches, including a mixed-quote case checked against the old code.

The focused regression build is still compiling dependencies. I also found that decorator facts come from `mro-members`; I’ll use that surface for the deep-chain regression and check the short control’s exact decorator fact.

The comment regression expects one block containing the full commented function: the opposite quote marker remains string content, so the following dedented payload line belongs to the docstring. For the coverage clusters, I’m checking observable facts against Python’s binding, inheritance, and exception rules.

The build is progressing through the analyzer and store crates; no test has run yet. The coverage cases will compare semantic fields and source spans, avoiding generated IDs so the assertions stay readable.
Compilation has reached the RQL crate. Once the old-code comment regression runs, I’ll record the failure, apply the delimiter fix, and run the new cases.

The old-code comment regression failed as expected: the block stopped at the opposite quote marker and omitted the docstring payload and return statement. The delimiter fix now tracks the opening quote style. I’ve also added coverage cases for constructors, raises, properties, lifecycle calls, cleanup, documentation, and range shadowing.

Four new cases pass, including the delimiter regression and constructor and raise checks. Five failed; I’ll inspect their diagnostics to distinguish test setup or schema mistakes from product defects, and stop any cluster that reveals another defect.

The lifecycle and range failures were test setup mistakes; those cases now pass. Decorated declarations need further investigation: the searches returned no decorated class members and mapped property methods to the class. I’ve saved the inputs and failures for the parent and stopped those clusters as instructed. Seven cases remain in the test module, and the full RQL library suite is running.

The path classification check passed. Clippy currently holds the Cargo build lock, so the library and policy commands are waiting behind it. The parent will need to decide how to test the deep decorator walk: `mro-members` returns no rows for the decorated class fixture.

The pack drift check passed with `core.autocrlf=false`. The default setting produced the known Node notice false positive; no pack content changed. Format checking passed too. Clippy has reached RQL, and I’ve saved the blocked cases, oracle notes, and test corrections in the report directory.
Clippy passed with warnings denied. The Python policy suite is compiling its remaining crates; the full RQL library run is still waiting for the build lock.

The policy build is still compiling. I’ve prepared one more coverage case for loop exits: break, continue, and return in the current iteration should affect redefinition analysis, while exits inside a nested function or inner loop should not.
All 261 Python policy tests passed. The RQL library suite is running and has passed more than 450 tests so far. I’ll wait for it to finish before adding and checking the loop-exit case.

The library suite finished with 639 passes and only the known Go failure named in the brief. The new loop case found another discrepancy: a return inside a nested function was treated as an exit from the current iteration. I’ll preserve that reproduction and stop the cluster as instructed, without changing production code.

Handed back three commits with both production fixes and seven passing tests. All 261 Python policy tests passed; the library suite had only the exempted Go failure.

Report includes blocked decorator/property coverage and a newly found nested-function exit defect.
I’ll fix the nested-scope exit check and restore its regression, add the decorator validation limit to a follow-up commit message, and write the property note. Then I’ll rerun the requested checks.

The restored regression fails on the old code at the nested-function case, and Git history identifies `409a4f663f49` as the commit that introduced the root exemption. The fix now skips scopes at every depth while preserving the existing loop-node rule. The property note is written; full library validation is running.

The nested-function case now passes. The restored inner-loop control exposed a separate problem: a direct inner `for` with `break` still yields `nested_loop_reused=true`. That follows from the loop-root exemption you explicitly asked me to preserve. I’ll hand back this conflict with the failure evidence and finish the independent validation checks.

All 261 Python policy tests pass again, along with Clippy, fmt, and pack drift. The library suite has two failures: the exempted Go test and the inner-loop control that conflicts with preserving the loop-root exemption. The changes are committed and the worktree is clean; I’ll hand back that decision with the patch, logs, and property note.

Committed `fd58b6e85f` and `b526af63cf`; handed back the patch, fail-before log, and property issue note.

Policy tests, Clippy, and fmt pass. The nested-function fix passes, but the inner-loop control fails because of the explicitly preserved loop-root exemption. That conflict needs your decision.
